content.overview: Verification asks whether an instrument is fit for a defined decision; calibration establishes measurement relationship to a suitable reference under an authorized method. The reference itself must be suitable and verified.

vocabulary.definition: A documented check that a device or measurement meets defined requirements for its intended use.
A controlled comparison to a suitable reference used to establish measurement relationship and, where authorized, adjustment.
Change in instrument response over time that can bias measurements.

sections.title: A second device is not automatically a reference
sections.body: Comparison instruments need their own suitability and verification status. An unverified handheld device cannot justify recalibration of a critical sensor.

sections.title: Stable offset and intermittent faults are different
sections.body: A consistent bias across checks suggests a different problem than step changes or state-dependent errors. Time-series behavior should guide the next verification.

sections.title: Preserve the original data
sections.body: Suspect measurements should be flagged and investigated, not silently rewritten to match an expected value.

workedExamples: A sensor passes one spot check but later shows impossible step changes; the spot check does not erase the intermittent data-quality concern.
commonMistakes: Using any convenient meter as a reference.
Treating verification and protected calibration as the same authority.
content.practicalApplication: Review a mock calibration history and classify each instrument as fit, limited, overdue or requiring qualified service.
content.summary: Calibration quality depends on reference quality, method control and traceable handling of drift and suspect data.
